case_study_insert.main_stem: Trek River Voyages (TRV) is a partnership in the tourism and leisure sector, running white-water rafting and river expedition holidays from a mountain basecamp and employing a workforce of 46. Founded in 2014 by Aisha Bhatt, TRV operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership so safety decisions are made quickly by experienced leaders. It plans to invest $560,000 in a new riverside basecamp and certified safety equipment, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $260,000 retained profit. TRV has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $25.00 a unit and a selling price of $40.00, and currently produces 24,000 units a year, each unit being one paid rafting place. A recent audit found a 4.5% defect rate in safety-kit checks and guide absenteeism is rising, raising concerns.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: TRV guided 6,200 rafting places last quarter at $40.00 each, with a 4.5% defect rate in pre-trip safety-kit checks, up from 2.8% a year ago. Guide absenteeism averaged 7 days a month across the team. Customer complaints rose from 12 to 27 per month. A survey of 450 adventure tourists found 61% rated safety as their top concern and 54% would pay $3.00 more for certified gear. Replacing a safety kit costs $75.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Trek River Voyages as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank increased the base interest rate from 4.0% to 5.25%, raising servicing costs on TRV's $300,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $12.80 to $13.72 per hour from April 2026, increasing the guide wage bill. (3) Specialised raft and safety-equipment input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year while tourism inflation is 5.9%, and adventure-holiday bookings grew 3.1%.

questions.question_text: TRV is funding its new riverside basecamp partly with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TRV of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $260,000 of retained profit costs TRV no interest or capital repayments, protecting cash flow while the partnership already carries fixed costs of $210,000 a year and a $300,000 loan. Every dollar saved on interest can fund the $75 safety-kit replacements needed to cut the 4.5% defect rate, or support the 46-strong team, keeping more of the $15.00 contribution from each rafting place.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the $560,000 basecamp and certified equipment cannot be seized if bookings fall. Aisha Bhatt and the partners also keep full control of the hierarchical structure and autocratic safety decisions without a lender imposing conditions. With guide absenteeism rising and complaints up to 27 a month, avoiding another fixed debt commitment gives TRV breathing room to put its safety record right before the new basecamp opens. The 1.25-point rise to 5.25% would add about $3,750 a year in interest on a variable-rate $300,000 loan, so avoiding that charge releases funds for the $75 safety-kit replacements and the 4.5% defect-rate campaign. It also gives the partnership more flexibility if the 11.3% equipment inflation persists.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TRV, its loan and its retained profit.

questions.question_text: TRV is promoting its new rafting basecamp. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TRV choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A TV campaign would quickly build awareness of white-water rafting across the country and could reach people who have never considered a river expedition. Yet airtime is very costly for a partnership with 46 staff already financing a $560,000 basecamp through debt, and most viewers live far from the mountain basecamp and cannot take a $40.00 rafting place, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and reaches the local catchment and passing tourists near the basecamp, and it suits short, urgent messages about the new safety-certified trips. Its limit is reach: the survey of 450 adventure tourists showed 61% care most about safety and demand comes from far beyond the local area, which radio cannot touch, so bookings would be capped.

Social media influencer marketing: Adventure and travel influencers can target exactly the 54% of surveyed tourists who would pay $3.00 more for certified gear, showing real footage of the rafting experience with measurable engagement at low cost. Results build more slowly than TV, but content can highlight the safety message that matters most.

Recommendation: TRV should choose social media influencer marketing. It speaks to the safety-conscious segment in the research, costs far less than television and reaches beyond local radio, all while promoting the certification that justifies the $560,000 investment. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; radio is rejected as too narrow for a national adventure market. Given that complaints have already risen from 12 to 27 a month, the promotion should only promise safety standards the 46 guides can deliver. A credible, low-cost digital campaign supports the certified-gear message without diverting scarce cash from the $560,000 basecamp.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TRV with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TRV with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Guide absenteeism is rising at TRV. Explain two benefits for TRV of using autocratic leadership to maintain safety standards.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Aisha Bhatt make firm, fast safety decisions without delay, which suits white-water rafting where the 4.5% defect rate in safety-kit checks must be corrected immediately. Clear instructions from the top reduce confusion among the 46 staff, cut the $75 cost of kit failures and protect the 6,200 rafting places sold last quarter, keeping the hierarchical structure effective when lives are at risk.

Point 2: A decisive leader can set non-negotiable attendance and check routines, directly tackling rising guide absenteeism and the jump in complaints from 12 to 27 a month. Because one leader drives standards, the 54% of surveyed tourists who would pay $3.00 more for certified gear can be assured of consistency, supporting the $40.00 price while the $560,000 basecamp and its equipment investment are bedded in. With 6,200 rafting places sold last quarter, a single serious safety failure would cost far more than a $75 kit, so decisive leadership is justified. Autocratic decisions also cut the delay that can arise in a hierarchical structure when guide absenteeism leaves crews short-handed.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TRV's defect rate, absenteeism and safety standards.

questions.question_text: TRV must cut its 4.5% defect rate in safety-kit checks. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local outdoor college. Which should TRV choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training guides on TRV's own safety kits and checking routines is directly relevant, costs no course fees and keeps the 46 staff productive on the river while they learn, which protects the 6,200 places sold last quarter and the drive to cut the 4.5% defect rate. The downside is that senior guides acting as trainers have less time for their own trips, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate to prove kit competence.

Off-the-job training: The local outdoor college can deliver structured checking procedures and a recognised certificate, valuable when 61% of surveyed tourists rank safety first and 54% would pay more for certified gear. However, it pulls guides off the river, reducing capacity during the launch, and the generic course may not match TRV's exact kits, so on-site follow-up would still be needed on return.

Decision: TRV should choose on-the-job training first, with short college certification for senior guides. It is cheaper, kit-specific and avoids losing river capacity while the defect rate is 4.5%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing many guides at once would disrupt trips and add fees on top of a $560,000 investment; college modules can be added once standards are stable. The real comparison is not the $75 kit price but lost river capacity: on-the-job coaching keeps the 46 guides working while defects stand at 4.5%. A short college qualification can be added for senior guides later, once the new basecamp is running and complaints are falling again. The college route remains a useful backup if on-site coaching cannot bring defects below 4.5% within the quarter.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TRV.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of TRV.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of TRV with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and safety relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TRV's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($40.00 − $25.00) = $210,000 ÷ $15.00 = 14,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 14,000 rafting-place units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $40.00 − $25.00 = $15.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $15.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TRV's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 14,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 24,000 units to confirm rafting is profitable, leaving a margin of safety of 10,000 places before the new basecamp is fully needed.
2. Contribution per unit of $15.00 lets TRV model the $3.00 price premium for certified gear in the survey; keeping that premium sustains contribution, while a discount would need higher volume to cover the $210,000 fixed costs.
3. The break-even figure helps Aisha Bhatt plan interest on the $300,000 loan for the $560,000 basecamp, checking that 24,000 places generate enough contribution before the partnership borrows again.
4. Average total cost of $33.75 a unit ($210,000 ÷ 24,000 + $25.00) can be tracked each quarter against the 4.5% safety-kit defect rate and rising guide absenteeism, so managers can target the $75 kit replacements and training where input costs have risen 11.3%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 14,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $15.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 24,000-unit output; pricing the $3.00 certified-gear premium; loan feasibility for the $560,000 basecamp; and average total cost benchmarking at $33.75 to tackle defects and absenteeism.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TRV's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TRV's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.64 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.39 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.14 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.86 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $70,000 inventories + $100,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $230,000; 2025 current assets = $95,000 + $130,000 + $25,000 = $250,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $230,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.64 and 2025 = $250,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.39. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($230,000 − $70,000) ÷ $140,000 = 1.14 and 2025 = ($250,000 − $95,000) ÷ $180,000 = 0.86.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly weakened. The 2024 figure of 1.64 fell to 1.39 as current liabilities jumped from $140,000 to $180,000 while cash fell from $60,000 to $25,000. The stricter measure, which removes inventories, dropped from 1.14 to 0.86, so TRV now cannot cover short-term debts without selling the growing $95,000 of stock — dangerous while it services a $300,000 loan and spends $560,000 on the basecamp. Trade receivables also rose from $100,000 to $130,000, tying up cash just when it is scarce.

Conclusion: TRV's financial position has not improved; it has deteriorated. Both measures fell (1.64 to 1.39 and 1.14 to 0.86) and the fall in cash is the main cause. TRV should delay further borrowing, chase the $130,000 of receivables and rebuild cash before committing fully to the $560,000 expansion. The weaker liquidity leaves little room for the 11.3% equipment inflation in the bulletin, so the partnership should rebuild cash before borrowing further. Chasing the $130,000 of receivables and slowing the $560,000 spend would protect the 14,000-unit break-even position.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether TRV's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TRV of replacing its safety equipment more frequently.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Replacing kits more often directly cuts the 4.5% defect rate found in checks, which matters because 61% of surveyed tourists rank safety first and 54% would pay $3.00 more for certified gear. Each kit costs $75, a small sum against the $40.00 price and the $560,000 basecamp, and better safety protects the reputation behind 6,200 places sold last quarter even as equipment input costs rise 11.3%.

Disadvantage: More frequent replacement adds to the $25.00 variable cost per unit and the $210,000 fixed costs at a time when the partnership services a $300,000 loan and has just seen liquidity worsen. Unless the $3.00 certified-gear premium is accepted widely, margins narrow; and if defects persist despite spending, the 27 monthly complaints could rise further, hurting the very safety image the investment is meant to protect. With 54% of surveyed tourists willing to pay $3.00 more, part of the $75 replacement cost can be recovered, but only if guests actually perceive the safety improvement. That depends on cutting the 4.5% defect rate and the 27 monthly complaints that currently damage TRV's reputation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TRV's survey, costs and safety record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in equipment input costs will affect TRV. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 5.25%): If TRV's $300,000 loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by 1.25% of $300,000 = $3,750 a year. That is modest beside fixed costs of $210,000, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is nil. Higher rates may still cool adventure-holiday demand, but TRV can cap the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $13.72 per hour): With a workforce of 46, most guide and support roles are hourly-paid, so the rise feeds into the wage bill. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest comparison is with the given output of 24,000 places across 46 staff, about 522 places per worker. If productivity holds and absenteeism is tackled, the $15.00 contribution can absorb it; if the 4.5% defect rate persists, unit labour costs climb.

Equipment input inflation (11.3%): The $25.00 variable cost per unit is where rafts and safety gear sit, but the insert gives no breakdown, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $25.00 rose 11.3%, that is 0.113 × $25.00 = $2.83 per unit, roughly $67,920 a year at 24,000 places. Even a $2.00-per-unit rise costs $48,000 a year, cutting contribution from $15.00 toward $13.00.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in equipment costs will have the greatest impact because it recurs on all 24,000 places and erodes the $15.00 contribution underpinning the $560,000 basecamp. The wage rise is meaningful but manageable if productivity holds, while the interest rise adds only about $3,750.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TRV.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TRV's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TRV with a well-justified judgment that equipment-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
